subject_line: An island festival as a test of integrity in The Brilliant & Forever
email_body:
Dear Kevin,

Reading about The Brilliant & Forever, I was struck by how the novel sets its story around an island literary festival and uses it to think about community, integrity and the act of writing itself. Reviewers called it absurdist and metafictional; it was also shortlisted for the Saltire Fiction Book of the Year.

I would like to ask how your work across novels, poetry and plays, and your teaching at Stirling, shape the way you think about writers being judged in public.

subject_line: Bardd y Dref cyntaf Aberystwyth a Llyfr Gwyrdd Ystwyth
email_body:
Annwyl Eurig,

Sylwais mai chi oedd Bardd y Dref cyntaf erioed Aberystwyth, yn 2023, a bod teitl eich cyfrol Llyfr Gwyrdd Ystwyth (Cyhoeddiadau Barddas, 2020) eisoes yn cyfeirio at yr ardal honno. Sylwais hefyd eich bod wedi cyd-olygu Y Gynghanedd Heddiw gydag Aneirin Karadog yr un flwyddyn.

Hoffwn ofyn sut mae bod yn Fardd y Dref wedi newid y ffordd rydych chi'n ysgrifennu am Aberystwyth, ac a yw'r gynghanedd yn gweddu i gerddi cyhoeddus o'r fath.

Prosiect annibynnol yw The Author Ledger sy'n cyhoeddi portreadau byr o awduron (Author Spotlights). Caiff pob portread ei ddatblygu drwy ychydig o gwestiynau ysgrifenedig, y gallwch eu hateb yn eich amser eich hun, a rhennir y testun llawn gyda chi i'w adolygu cyn ei gyhoeddi.

Fyddech chi'n fodlon cymryd rhan?

Cofion gorau,
The Author Ledger

subject_line: Your grandfather, Beckett and the letters behind Jott
email_body:
Dear Sam,

I read that Jott grew partly out of real letters from a 1930s friendship between your grandfather and Samuel Beckett, and that the novel turned that material into a story about friendship, madness and modernism, later shortlisted for the Encore Prize. You have since moved into children's fiction too, with Wolfstongue winning a Spark School Book Award in 2022.

I would like to ask how family papers became fiction in Jott, and what changes for you when you write for younger readers.

subject_line: Anna Sewell, the Rebel Writers and a novelist turned biographer
email_body:
Dear Celia,

After nine novels, your recent books have turned to other writers: Rebel Writers (2019) studied seven women who debuted in the late 1950s and early 1960s, and Writing Black Beauty (2023) follows Anna Sewell and the making of that novel. It is an interesting arc for someone whose own fiction, such as Wild Weekend, reworked She Stoops to Conquer in a Suffolk village.

I would like to ask whether years of writing fiction changed how you read the decisions Sewell made.

subject_line: Watching the weather over the flatlands near Goole
email_body:
Dear Anthony,

I was drawn to Weatherman: the flatlands around Goole, with a central character who watches the weather. It sits interestingly beside Jack and Sal, where a couple drifting in and out of love is told through micro-stories, and beside your radio play I'll Tell You About Love, which won the BBC Alfred Bradley Award.

I would like to ask how a flat, exposed landscape shaped the pace of Weatherman, and whether radio drama changed how you build scenes on the page.

book_title: The Earlie King & the Kid in Yellow
subject_line: Myth, play scripts and a gangster saga in The Earlie King & the Kid in Yellow
email_body:
Dear Danny,

What stood out to me in The Earlie King & the Kid in Yellow is how the novel builds its dystopian Irish gangster saga out of mixed parts: fragments of poetry, Irish myth and play scripts. One reviewer even suggested it might suit the stage.

I would like to ask how you decided which parts of the story needed a script or a poem rather than prose, and whether editing The Stinging Fly from 2018 to 2022 changed how you think about form.

subject_line: From The Road, Slowly to the forthcoming Halfway Home
email_body:
Dear Liz,

I noticed the arc of your Salmon Poetry titles: The Road, Slowly in 2018, How We Arrive in Winter in 2021, which The Irish Times chose among the best poetry collections of that year, and Halfway Home, listed as forthcoming. Read together, the titles feel like stages of a single journey.

I would like to ask whether you see the collections as connected in that way, and how teaching creative writing at UCC sits alongside writing the third.

subject_line: The caller and the empty farmhouse in This Plague of Souls
email_body:
Dear Mike,

This Plague of Souls opens with John Nealon coming home to an empty farmhouse under the Sheeffry Hills in Mayo, only for a stranger on the phone to offer news of his family in exchange for a conversation. Reviewers described it as part-noir, part-metaphysical cat-and-mouse, and noted it is your shortest novel at 179 pages.

I would like to ask why this story needed to be so compressed, and what keeps drawing your fiction back to the Mayo of your childhood.

subject_line: The harpers of 1792 in Conditional Perfect
email_body:
Dear Emily,

I was struck that several poems in Conditional Perfect return to Belfast in 1792, when harpers gathered for the Belfast Harpers Assembly, and that some are monologues in those harpers' voices. Alongside them, the collection takes up motherhood, family and the politics of silence, and The Irish Times counted it among the best new poetry of 2019.

As a harpist yourself, I would like to ask how playing the instrument shaped the way you imagined those voices.

subject_line: Balor, Eithne and the women's voices in The Poison Glen
email_body:
Dear Annemarie,

In The Poison Glen, the legend of Balor and Eithne runs through forty poems about silenced mothers and foundlings, and you have spoken about wanting the women's perspectives at the centre. Reviewers also noted how the book is rooted in the Donegal Gaeltacht and continues the work of Bloodroot.

I would like to ask how the old myth helped you hold such personal and public material, and how your residency at UCD in 2025 has shaped what came next.

subject_line: From flash fiction bananas to the picaresque of Cole the Magnificent
email_body:
Dear Tony,

Your work moves across unusually different forms: the visual sonnet sequence All the Rooms of Uncle's Head, a Poetry Book Society Pamphlet Choice; the flash fiction of All the Bananas I've Never Eaten, which won a Saboteur Award; and now Cole the Magnificent (2023), a picaresque novel.

I would like to ask what the picaresque, with its episodic, wandering shape, allowed you to do that poems and very short fiction could not, and whether the flash pieces trained you for it.
